name: Ruy Lopez
tagline: 3.Bb5: slow pressure on e5 and a long-term grip on the centre.
description: A complete White repertoire after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. You play the classical Closed Ruy: castle, Re1, c3 and h3, then d4 with a big, safe centre and a knight tour to g3. Against the Berlin you choose the quiet 4.d3, and against the Schliemann the calm 4.d3 as well, so you avoid the sharpest theory. The plans repeat across lines — c3 and d4, the Nbd2-f1-g3 manoeuvre, Bxc6 and Nxe5 when e5 is loose — and every common sideline comes with the trap that club players fall into.

chapters.name: Closed Main Line
chapters.intro: The heart of the Ruy Lopez. White castles, protects e4 with Re1 and builds the c3–d4 centre. The quiet 9.h3 stops ...Bg4, so the f3-knight keeps defending d4. Black chooses a plan: ...Na5 and ...c5 (Chigorin), the knight tour ...Nb8-d7 (Breyer), or ...Bb7 and ...Re8 (Zaitsev). Our plan barely changes: d4, Nbd2-f1-g3, and a4 or d5 when the moment is right. Remember the bishop on b3 or c2 is our best piece, and the d5 push closes the centre so we can play on the side where we have more space.

quiz.question: Why does White play 9.h3 before d4?
options: To prepare g4 and a kingside attack
To stop ...Bg4, so the f3-knight can keep supporting d4
To give the king an escape square
quiz.explanation: If Black could pin the knight with ...Bg4, the d4 pawn would lose a key defender. h3 makes d4 safe and keeps our centre solid.

options: To avoid the Marshall Attack, 8.c3 d5

chapters.name: Fifth- and Sixth-Move Alternatives
chapters.intro: Before the main line, Black has several sound alternatives. Against an early ...Bc5 (Møller and Arkhangelsk) we play c3 and d4 to hit the bishop with pawns, then Be3 to trade it. Against ...d6 lines we keep the same c3-d4 centre. The most important trap is 6...O-O?: with Re1 protecting e4, Bxc6 and Nxe5 wins a clean pawn. Many of these lines transpose back into the main line, so recognise the familiar positions.

chapters.name: Open Ruy Lopez
chapters.intro: In the Open Ruy, Black takes on e4 and gets free development. We answer with 6.d4 to open lines while Black’s king is in the centre. After ...b5, ...d5 and ...Be6 we push dxe5, put pawns on c3, and fight for the d4 square with Nbd2-b3 or Nd4. The knight on e4 is Black’s pride, but it can also become a target. chapters.name: Berlin Defence: 4.d3
chapters.intro: Against the Berlin we avoid the famous endgame with the quiet 4.d3. We protect e4 with a pawn, play c3, castle, Re1 and h3, then route the knight Nbd2-f1-g3, the same plan as in the Closed Ruy. The bishop drops back to a4 and c2 if attacked. Black often plays ...Bc5; keep a retreat ready for our bishop and the d4 push in reserve. Punish loose moves: ...a6 too early lets Bxc6 and Nxe5 win a pawn.

quiz.question: What is White’s plan against the Steinitz Deferred?
options: c3 and d4 to build a big centre
quiz.explanation: With ...d6 Black has protected e5 but given us time. c3 and d4 take the centre while the bishop on a4 keeps a safe retreat on c2.

chapters.name: Third-Move Sidelines
chapters.intro: Black has many alternatives on move three. Against the Classical (3...Bc5) we castle and play c3 and d4 to hit the bishop with pawns. Against the Schliemann (3...f5) we play the calm 4.d3: after ...fxe4 dxe4 our pieces develop easily and e6 is a weak spot. Against the Steinitz (3...d6) we take the centre with d4. Against the Bird (3...Nd4) we trade and attack the lone d4 pawn. In every line, keep an eye on Bxc6 and Nxe5 when e5 runs out of defenders.

Bg5 { Pin the knight; Nd5 comes next. } 8... d6 9. Nd5 { A dream square: the knight hits f6 and c7, and the light squares around Black's king are weak. }

lines.name: Steinitz: 3...d6 Tarrasch Trap
lines.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 { Develops with an attack on e5. } 2... Nc6 3. Bb5 { The Ruy Lopez. The bishop attacks the knight that defends e5. Nothing is threatened yet, but the pressure lasts the whole game. } 3... d6 { The old Steinitz Defence: solid but passive. } 4. d4 { Take the centre and attack e5 a second time. } 4... Bd7 5. Nc3 Nf6 6. O-O Be7 7. Re1 { e5 is attacked three times. Black must take on d4. } 7... O-O { A famous mistake. } 8. Bxc6 Bxc6 9. dxe5 dxe5 10. Qxd8 Raxd8 11. Nxe5 Bxe4 12. Nxe4 Nxe4 13. Nd3 { Threatens f3, trapping the knight on e4. Black cannot save everything and loses material. }

lines.pgn: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 { Develops with an attack on e5. } 2... Nc6 3. Bb5 { The Ruy Lopez. The bishop attacks the knight that defends e5. Nothing is threatened yet, but the pressure lasts the whole game. } 3... g6 { Black plans ...Bg7. } 4. d4 { Hit the centre before the bishop arrives. } 4... exd4 5. Bg5 { Annoying: the bishop hits the queen and stops ...Bg7 for now. } 5... Be7 6. Bxe7 Qxe7 7. Bxc6 dxc6 8. Qxd4 { We win back the pawn and Black's dark squares on f6 and h6 are weak. }

quiz.question: Black castled. How does White win material?
quiz.explanation: The Tarrasch Trap. After 8.Bxc6 Bxc6 9.dxe5 dxe5 10.Qxd8 Raxd8 11.Nxe5 Bxe4 12.Nxe4 Nxe4 13.Nd3, the e4 knight is short of squares and Black loses material.

quiz.question: Where does White’s knight belong in this Schliemann line?
quiz.explanation: After ...f5 and ...fxe4 the light squares are weak. Nd5 doubles the pressure on the pinned f6 knight and also eyes c7.

quiz.question: What does 9.a4 threaten?
options: a5, attacking the bishop on b6
Nothing; it is a waiting move
quiz.explanation: With the bishop on b6, a4-a5 gains space and drives it back. Black has to spend a move on ...a6 or ...a5.
